analysis.one_liner: Makes police chokeholds and carotid restraints a federal criminal civil rights violation.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would make chokeholds a federal civil rights violation, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Named for Eric Garner, who died in 2014 after a New York police officer put him in a chokehold, this bill would change federal criminal civil rights law to say that a police officer using a chokehold, carotid hold, or any maneuver restricting breathing or blood flow to the brain is committing a civil rights violation. That would give federal prosecutors a clearer tool to charge officers who use these restraints. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who come into contact with police — the bill would make it easier for federal prosecutors to charge officers who use chokeholds or carotid restraints, techniques that have repeatedly killed people in police custody. Families of victims of police violence would gain a clearer federal legal remedy.

how_it_helps.text: It adds language to 18 U.S.C. 242 stating that applying pressure to the throat or windpipe, restricting blood or oxygen flow to the brain, or using carotid artery restraints is a 'deprivation of a right' and a 'punishment, pain, or penalty' by a government official.
This would let federal prosecutors charge officers who use chokeholds under the existing criminal civil rights statute, which currently does not name specific restraint techniques.

analysis.who_pays: Police officers and the law enforcement agencies and unions that defend chokehold and carotid hold techniques; they would face federal criminal civil rights exposure when officers use these restraints.

drawbacks.text: The bill amends a criminal statute, so it would expose individual officers to federal prosecution; critics of expanding criminal liability for police argue this can chill decisive action in violent encounters.

Because it only defines chokeholds under an existing federal criminal civil rights statute, the bill depends on federal prosecutors bringing cases; it does not itself ban chokeholds by state or local police departments or create any independent enforcement mechanism.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy is narrow and targeted: it does not ban police use of force generally, it only classifies chokeholds and similar restraints as civil rights violations under an existing criminal statute, so the cost to legitimate policing is minimal and the benefit — removing a lethal technique that has repeatedly killed people — is clear. The real weakness is enforcement: the bill relies on federal criminal prosecution of individual officers, which is rare, and the bill never received a hearing or vote, so its actual benefit was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Gillibrand introduced the bill on February 4, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The action history shows no further activity after the committee referral; the bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments and officers retain the ability to use chokeholds and carotid restraints without federal criminal civil rights exposure; no member of the public gained any new protection.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no other senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Police unions and law enforcement groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal legislation expanding criminal liability for police use-of-force during the 2020-2021 policing debate, contributing to the lack of Republican support for such measures.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a recorded vote; it had zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan position was ever formally expressed.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies and police unions
industries.note: The bill would give federal prosecutors a clearer path to criminally charge officers who use chokeholds or carotid restraints, ending a practice many departments still authorize or tolerate.
